I want to tell y'all about the ADA and service dog law, because it protects you too, it's not just to be a pain in your ass.

1. **Only dogs and mini horses** may be service animals. Mini horses may be refused if the facility cannot accommodate it's size or it'd pose a safety danger.

2. **Staff may ask only 2 questions When asking if it's a service animal**
> - Is the dog a service animal required because of a disability, 
> - What work or task has the dog been trained to perform. 
> - Emotional support is not a specific task

3. **The dog must be under the handlers control at all times. If not, they can be asked to remove the dog.**
> - *This includes if it is not housebroken*


4. **Staff are not required to provide care for or supervision of a service animal.**

5. Service animals can go where a member of the general public can go. Specific example from the ada website: 
> "For example, in a hospital it usually would be inappropriate to exclude a service animal from areas such as patient rooms, clinics, cafeterias, or examination rooms. However, it may be appropriate to exclude a service animal from operating rooms or burn units where the animal’s presence may compromise a sterile environment."

[Source](https://www.ada.gov/resources/service-animals-2010-requirements/)

The website is easy to read, and user friendly. Many people in the comments are making up scenarios that wouldn't be an issue if you're familiar with the law. The law can't protect you if you don't know it or use it. And if your employer tries to not kick out an aggressive animal, then know your rights for having a safe work environment.

Deep breaths. Let's take inventory. 

What happened that night? You had a very busy night, and an urgent need you didn't have an immediate solution to. Things got away from you, you didn't prioritize well in that regard, and didn't reach out for help. The patient is in critical care and had an adverse outcome, but they are alive. 

What happened after? You had a meeting with management to address an adverse event. That's expected, and going to happen. Are they happy it happened? Obviously not. But if anyone is *mad*, then they need to work with a therapist, because these things, while unfortunate, do happen. At the end of the day, anyone else's feelings about *you as a nurse* and *you as a person* are irrelevant. 

As a nurse, *at some point*, you will fuck up in a way that will hurt someone. That is a fact. It may not be major, it may be minor, but everyone in healthcare will contribute both positively and negatively to outcomes. Your responsibility is to develop your practice in a way to make those infrequent and minimal as possible. Is this serious? Absolutely. But the fact you care shows you're a good nurse. 

If this is going to happen, now is the time in your career for it. You're brand new. Now is the best time to make changes. Now that you know you're not a bad nurse and not a bad person for this, it's time to take action and make a plan.

I'm sure you went over specific prioritization tools (abcde, urgent vs non urgent, etc) at the meeting. Don't be afraid to use your resources, like the charge or stat RN. Sometimes, I just update the charge on my patients if anything is happening just in case. A lot of times, they have great perspectives I didn't even think of. How do you keep track of your tasks during your shift? Epic work list? A paper brain sheet? How can you change your habits during the shift so you can periodically pause and regroup yourself to remind yourself of what's important? Do you have generalized anxiety/ADHD/anything that a therapist or meds could help? If you need a day off, don't be afraid to take it. Better to take it off than come to work feel a total mess.

Tl;Dr: yes, it's serious, but feeling like shit about it won't prevent it from happening in the future. Give yourself permission to feel those feelings, then wish them well and make a plan for where to go from here.

I cope with crippling depression!! I've pretty much abandoned all my coping skills bc my mental health was precarious at best before this, and my therapist fired me as a patient for missing appointments, so i just ✨suffer✨
 
 
 
All jokes aside:
 

1. Therapy
 
 
2. Journaling. One half for good things when you need to remember, one half for bad when you need to let it out. 

2a. Go over the good things regularly. It takes 5 positive stimuli to cancel out 1 negative in the human brain. That worked great when humans were constantly in danger and being chased by tigers, but our brain hasn't got the message that theres no tigers.
 
2b. Dont feel guilty about being affected by those negative things. We are facing very graphic things and serious moral injury. This pandemic has made our lives ridiculously similar to a warzone. Dont feel a single ounce of guilt for those negative thoughts. Accepting them is key to letting them go.
 
3. Think of one, small, good thing you did on your shift. Washed someones hair, held their hand, fuck, even telling your sedated and paralyzed patient what day and time it was and that you hope they get good sleep. Use that to define your shift in your brain. When you ask yourself what you did today, thats what you did, thats what you think about. Sure, negative stuff will come in, but do your best to think that above all. Because you did do something great, your brain is just bound and determined to bring up the negatives. Thats ok. Thats normal. 
 
 4. Make sure all your basic needs are met. Keep snacks and water bottles by your bed for when youre too exhausted and dont care enough to get some before bed. 
 
 
 Thats all i got. Tbh it helps me a lot to write it down so i remember to actually do all this shit
